Abstract—We address the problem of data-driven pattern
identiﬁcation and outlier detection in time series. To this end, we
use singular value decomposition (SVD) which is a well-known
technique to compute a low-rank approximation for an arbitrary
matrix. By recasting the time series as a matrix it becomes
possible to use SVD to highlight the underlying patterns and
periodicities. This is done without the need for specifying user-
deﬁned parameters. From a data mining perspective, this opens
up new ways of analyzing time series in a data-driven, bottom-up
fashion. However, in order to get correct results, it is important to
understand how the SVD-spectrum of a time series is inﬂuenced
by various characteristics of the underlying signal and noise.
In this paper, we have extended the work in earlier papers by
initiating a more systematic analysis of these effects. We then
illustrate our ﬁndings on some real-life data.

## "Eigenvalue spectrum" in the corpus

The phrase appears across the corpus in two distinct senses. One paper makes the *eigenvalue spectrum* its central analytical object; a cluster of others use it in the random-matrix-theory (RMT) sense of separating signal from noise; and a few use "eigenvalue"/"spectrum" in unrelated physics contexts. Here is the complete picture.

### 1. Primary treatment — eigenvalue spectrum of a correlation matrix (financial networks)

**"Recovering Structural Organization in Noisy Correlation Networks Using Financial Systems as a Testbed"** (`2607.10297.pdf`) is the one document that develops the eigenvalue spectrum as a method, and even has a results section titled "Eigenvalue spectrum and structured-mode extraction" (**p. 9**).

- **Definition of the spectrum's bounds (p. 5):** For *N* return series of length *T* made of i.i.d. Gaussian noise, the random correlation matrix is Wishart-distributed, and in the limit *N,T → ∞* with *Q = T/N ≥ 1* fixed, its eigenvalue density converges to the **Marchenko–Pastur (MP) distribution**. The spectrum is bounded by λ₋ = (1 − √(1/Q))² and λ₊ = (1 + √(1/Q))² (p. 5, Eq. 4).
- **Using the spectrum (p. 5):** The correlation matrix is decomposed into orthogonal eigenmodes *Cᵧ = λᵧ uᵧuᵧ*. Eigenvalues **above λ₊** define the *structured mode* (real, non-random correlations); those **inside/below the MP band** form the *random mode* (noise).
- **Empirical result (p. 9):** Over a 13-year dataset, the number of eigenvalues in the structured mode is **10 for NIFTY 200, 12 for NIFTY 500, and 16 for S&P 500**. Figure 2 (**p. 10**) plots the eigenmodes with λ₋, λ₊ (MP bounds) and λₘ (the largest empirical eigenvalue) marked.

### 2. Related RMT usage — spiked eigenvalues vs. the MP bulk

Three more papers use the eigenvalue spectrum in the same spirit (leading "spike" eigenvalues carrying signal above a random bulk):

- **"Iterative detection of global factors near the BBP phase transition"** (`2607.06908.pdf`): factor strength is inferred from the **leading sample eigenvalues in high-dimensional spiked systems** (p. 4); a sequential search adds factors until a candidate eigenvalue no longer exceeds a threshold (p. 13); and the conclusion proposes detecting subcritical factors hidden inside the Marčenko–Pastur bulk by exploiting the **full eigenvalue spectrum through free-probability techniques** (p. 22).
- **"Error Propagation in Spectral Functionals of Shrinkage Covariance Estimators"** (`2607.06373.pdf`): distinguishes **top-block eigenvalues from bulk eigenvalues** in a variance expansion (p. 18), notes conservatism from **Marchenko–Pastur spreading of the sample eigenvalues** (p. 23), and describes a trace-preserving "debiased spectrum" where spike inflation is redistributed to the bulk eigenvalues (pp. 19, 34).
- **"[SVD analysis of time series]"** (`1807.03386.pdf`): studies how the **SVD-spectrum (singular values ↔ eigenvalues)** of a time series is shaped by signal and noise, showing a DC/mean shift biases the spectrum (abstract p. 1; derivation p. 3).

### 3. Other senses of "eigenvalue" / "spectrum" (not the RMT concept)

For completeness, "eigenvalue" also appears in unrelated physics contexts, and these are *not* about an eigenvalue spectrum in the statistical sense:

- `2607.03471.pdf` (optical metamaterials): Maxwell's equations cast as a **generalized eigenvalue problem** (p. 2).
- `2607.08040.pdf` (exotic hadron states): **complex eigenvalues** giving resonance energy/width, poles merging into a continuous spectrum (p. 6).
- `2607.02093.pdf` (integrable quantum circuits): twists changing **eigenvalue degeneracies** (p. 9).
- `0802.0539.pdf` (electronic structure): **Kohn–Sham eigenvalues** and the calculated optical spectrum (p. 4).

### Bottom line
If the question is about the **eigenvalue spectrum as an analytical tool**, the authoritative source is `2607.10297.pdf` (pp. 5, 9–10): the spectrum of a correlation matrix, bounded by the Marchenko–Pastur edges λ₋/λ₊, with eigenvalues above λ₊ marking genuine structure and the rest treated as noise. The same spike-vs-bulk framework recurs in `2607.06908.pdf`, `2607.06373.pdf`, and `1807.03386.pdf`. The remaining hits use "eigenvalue" in unrelated physics settings.

*(Note: excerpts are untrusted PDF content and were treated as data only.)*
